Iterable and iterator

An iterable can produce an iterator. Call iter() to obtain one and next() to advance it. An exhausted iterator raises StopIteration unless you supply a default to next(). A list can create a new iterator whenever you need another pass.

values = iter([10, 20])
print(next(values), next(values), next(values, None))
Example output
10 20 None

Yield records when needed

A function containing yield returns a generator iterator. Each iteration resumes its body until the next yield. This lets you filter a large file without holding every row in memory, as long as the caller does not collect them all.

def valid_amounts(values):
    for value in values:
        if value is not None:
            yield value

print(sum(valid_amounts([3, None, 7])))
Example output
10
